ssh_server.exposure: Heavily targeted by automated scanners and brute-force attacks — internet-exposed by default
ssh_server.threat: Full shell access to the machine, privilege escalation, lateral movement to other network systems

vnc_server.exposure: Often lacks native encryption; weak or absent authentication on older versions
vnc_server.threat: Full visual and interactive desktop control — equivalent to physical access to the machine

ftp_server.exposure: Unencrypted protocol — credentials and data transmitted in plain text over the network
ftp_server.threat: Credential theft, file access and exfiltration, potential pivot if credentials are reused

postgresql.exposure: Password or configurable authentication — direct exposure is rarely intentional
postgresql.threat: Full database exfiltration, system command execution via extensions (pg_execute_server_program)

redis.exposure: No authentication by default historically, very frequently misconfigured and exposed
redis.threat: Read/write access to all data, remote code execution (RCE) via configuration — documented and actively exploited attack vector

wireguard_vpn.exposure: Intentionally internet-facing for VPN function — limited attack surface by design
wireguard_vpn.threat: Full internal network access if tunnel is compromised or private keys are stolen

home_assistant.exposure: Web interface controlling physical devices — built-in authentication but often exposed for remote access
home_assistant.threat: Control of physical devices (locks, alarms, switches), local network access via automations, home automation data exfiltration

nextcloud.exposure: Personal file server exposed to the internet — authentication required but significant attack surface depending on installed apps
nextcloud.threat: Access to all personal files, contacts and calendars stored, potential pivot if credentials are compromised

samba_windows_file_sharing.exposure: Designed exclusively for local networks — inherently dangerous if exposed to the internet
samba_windows_file_sharing.threat: File access and encryption (ransomware), lateral movement (EternalBlue/WannaCry), data exfiltration

mysql___mariadb.exposure: Password-based authentication, history of unauthenticated access CVEs
mysql___mariadb.threat: Full database exfiltration, data destruction, application-level access if credentials are shared

cockpit_web_admin.exposure: Web-based system administration interface — authentication required but significant attack surface
cockpit_web_admin.threat: Full system administration if compromised: service management, users, network, root terminal

mosquitto_mqtt.exposure: MQTT broker often without authentication by default, listens on all interfaces
mosquitto_mqtt.threat: Unauthorised publish/subscribe to home automation topics, device control, sensor data interception

apache_web_server.exposure: Web server potentially exposed to the internet — commonly targeted by automated vulnerability scanners
apache_web_server.threat: Web application exploits, path traversal, remote code execution if CGI or modules are misconfigured

nginx_web_server.exposure: Web server potentially exposed to the internet — commonly targeted by automated vulnerability scanners
nginx_web_server.threat: Web application exploits, reverse proxy misconfigurations leading to internal service exposure

transmission_web_ui.exposure: Web interface for BitTorrent client — unauthenticated access by default on older versions
transmission_web_ui.threat: Remote control of downloads, potential RCE via malicious torrents if exposed publicly

qbittorrent_web_ui.exposure: Web interface for BitTorrent client — default credentials (admin/adminadmin) frequently unchanged
qbittorrent_web_ui.threat: Remote control of downloads, file system write access via download directory configuration

avahi_local_network_discovery.exposure: mDNS/DNS-SD service — designed for local network use only, not internet-facing
avahi_local_network_discovery.threat: Local network device and service enumeration — low risk on isolated or properly firewalled networks

cups_network_printing.exposure: Print server — typically restricted to local network, not intended for internet exposure
cups_network_printing.threat: Printer access and configuration disclosure on local network — minimal risk if not publicly exposed

jellyfin.exposure: Media server web interface — may be exposed for remote streaming access
jellyfin.threat: Unauthorised media access, potential RCE if outdated versions with known CVEs are running

plex_media_server.exposure: Media server with cloud relay — phone-home by default, may be directly accessible if port-forwarded
plex_media_server.threat: Unauthorised media access, metadata exposure, potential RCE on outdated versions

gitea.exposure: Self-hosted Git service — may contain private repositories, credentials and CI/CD secrets
gitea.threat: Source code and secret exfiltration, arbitrary code execution via Git hooks if admin account is compromised

syncthing.exposure: Peer-to-peer file sync — web UI bound to localhost by default, sync protocol may be externally reachable
syncthing.threat: File access and modification, directory traversal if misconfigured, data synchronisation interception

ollama_llm_server.exposure: Local LLM API server — no authentication by default, designed for local or trusted network use
ollama_llm_server.threat: Unauthorised model inference, resource exhaustion, potential data exfiltration via model prompts

telnet_server.exposure: Unencrypted plaintext protocol — credentials, commands and all data transmitted in clear text over the network
telnet_server.threat: Credential theft in transit, session hijacking, trivial interception on any network segment — replace with SSH immediately

rdp___xrdp.exposure: Remote desktop protocol — primary target of ransomware operators and automated scanners (BlueKeep, DejaBlue CVEs)
rdp___xrdp.threat: Full graphical desktop access, credential theft, ransomware deployment, lateral movement to other systems

mongodb.exposure: No authentication by default in older versions — hundreds of thousands of unprotected instances found publicly exposed
mongodb.threat: Full database read/write access, data exfiltration and destruction, potential code execution via server-side JavaScript

elasticsearch.exposure: No authentication in open-source version by default — frequently misconfigured and indexed publicly by Shodan
elasticsearch.threat: Full exfiltration of all indexed documents, index deletion, cluster takeover — requires X-Pack Security or equivalent

memcached.exposure: No authentication, UDP enabled by default — actively abused for DDoS amplification attacks (factor up to 50,000x)
memcached.threat: Cache poisoning and data exfiltration, amplification DDoS vector against third parties, service disruption

kernel_hardening.kptr_exposed: Kernel pointers exposed in /proc (kptr_restrict=0) — may leak kernel addresses to unprivileged users
kernel_hardening.kptr_exposed_detail: When kptr_restrict=0, kernel symbol addresses appear in /proc files and can be read by unprivileged users, making KASLR bypass much easier.
kernel_hardening.dmesg_ok: dmesg access restricted to privileged users (dmesg_restrict=1)
kernel_hardening.dmesg_exposed: dmesg accessible to all users (dmesg_restrict=0) — kernel messages may reveal exploitable information
kernel_hardening.dmesg_exposed_detail: When dmesg_restrict=0, any local user can read kernel log messages, which may reveal memory layout, loaded modules, or hardware details useful for exploitation.

suid_audit.scan_skipped: SUID/SGID scan timed out or failed — check skipped
suid_audit.ok: All SUID binaries are known-safe ({suid_count} SUID, {sgid_count} SGID)
suid_audit.unexpected_suid_detail: These binaries run as root regardless of who launches them. Verify each one is intentional, then either remove the SUID bit (chmod u-s) or add it to your local whitelist.
suid_audit.unexpected_sgid_detail: SGID binaries run with the file's group privileges. Less dangerous than SUID but worth reviewing.

docker_audit.scan_error: Docker daemon not reachable — container security check skipped
docker_audit.no_containers: No running containers — nothing to audit
docker_audit.ok: {count} running container(s) — no critical security issues found
docker_audit.privileged_detail: Privileged containers have full access to the host kernel and devices. This effectively disables container isolation. Replace with fine-grained capabilities (--cap-add) if elevated privileges are required.
docker_audit.socket_mounted_detail: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock inside a container grants root-equivalent control over the host. Any process in the container can create new privileged containers or escape the sandbox.
docker_audit.userns_not_configured_detail: Without userns-remap, a container process running as UID 0 maps directly to root on the host. Enable userns-remap in /etc/docker/daemon.json to remap container UIDs away from root.
docker_audit.root_containers_detail: Running containers as root increases the blast radius of a container escape. Set a non-root USER in the Dockerfile or pass --user at runtime.
docker_audit.host_network_detail: Containers in host network mode share the host's network stack and can bind to any port. Use bridge networking and publish only required ports.

kernel_modules.no_lsmod: lsmod not available — kernel module check skipped
kernel_modules.risky_fs_detail: These modules are rarely needed on a server and widen the attack surface. Unload and blacklist them.
kernel_modules.risky_net_detail: These protocols (DCCP, SCTP, RDS, TIPC) are rarely used and have a history of kernel exploits. Unload and blacklist them.

kernel_modules.kernels_reboot_pending_detail:
Installed: {installed}
Do not remove old kernels yet. Reboot into {recent} first and verify the system works correctly.
kernel_modules.kernels_update_available: Kernel update available ({candidate} in apt repository)
kernel_modules.kernels_up_to_date: Kernel {version} — up to date in the apt repository

cron_audit.pipe_to_shell: {count} cron job(s) pipe remote content into a shell (curl/wget | sh)
cron_audit.pipe_to_shell_detail: Piping remote downloads directly into a shell is a common supply-chain attack vector. Review and replace with explicit script downloads and integrity checks.
cron_audit.pipe_to_shell_reason: {count} cron job(s) pipe remote content into a shell
cron_audit.world_writable: {count} script(s) referenced in cron are world-writable: {scripts}
cron_audit.world_writable_detail: World-writable scripts can be replaced by any local user, enabling privilege escalation. Restrict permissions immediately.
cron_audit.ok: No risky patterns found in cron jobs

services_state.no_systemctl: systemctl not available — service state check skipped
services_state.service_inactive: Security service enabled but not running: {service}
services_state.service_inactive_detail: This service is set to start at boot but is currently stopped or failed. Check its logs and restart it.
services_state.ok: All monitored security services are active

password_auth.title: Password authentication enabled (PasswordAuthentication yes)
password_auth.why: Allows anyone to attempt to guess passwords via brute force. Millions of bots scan the internet 24/7 trying common passwords against SSH port 22. A weak or reused password is all it takes for a full compromise.
password_auth.how:
1. Generate a key pair if you don't have one:
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519
2. Copy your public key to the server:
   ssh-copy-id user@server
3. Disable password auth:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PasswordAuthentication no
4. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

permit_root_login.title: Root SSH login permitted (PermitRootLogin)
permit_root_login.why: Direct root login bypasses audit trails and gives full system access from the first connection. If an attacker guesses or steals the root credential, no further privilege escalation is needed — the server is fully compromised immediately.
permit_root_login.how:
1. Ensure a regular user with sudo rights exists
2. Disable root login:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PermitRootLogin no
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

permit_empty_passwords.title: Empty passwords allowed (PermitEmptyPasswords yes)
permit_empty_passwords.why: Any account without a password is directly accessible over SSH with a blank password. This is an immediate full-access vulnerability requiring zero effort from an attacker.
permit_empty_passwords.how:
1. Disable empty passwords:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PermitEmptyPasswords no
2. Lock accounts with empty passwords:
   sudo passwd -l <username>
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

allow_tcp_forwarding.title: TCP forwarding enabled (AllowTcpForwarding yes)
allow_tcp_forwarding.why: TCP forwarding lets any authenticated user tunnel arbitrary TCP traffic through SSH. An attacker with a valid account can pivot to internal services that are not directly reachable from the internet.
allow_tcp_forwarding.how:
1. Disable TCP forwarding:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  AllowTcpForwarding no
2. If specific users need port forwarding, use:
   AllowTcpForwarding local
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

pubkey_auth_disabled.title: Public key authentication disabled (PubkeyAuthentication no)
pubkey_auth_disabled.why: Disabling public key authentication forces all users onto password login. This removes the strongest authentication mechanism available and makes the server entirely dependent on password strength.
pubkey_auth_disabled.how:
1. Enable key-based authentication:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PubkeyAuthentication yes
2. Generate a key pair:
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519
3. Copy the key to the server:
   ssh-copy-id user@server
4. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

x11_forwarding.title: X11 forwarding enabled (X11Forwarding yes)
x11_forwarding.why: X11 forwarding exposes your local X11 display to a remote server. A malicious or compromised remote host could capture keystrokes and screen contents from your X session.
x11_forwarding.how:
1. Disable X11 forwarding:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  X11Forwarding no
2. If genuinely needed, ensure X11UseLocalhost yes is also set
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

dsa_key.title: DSA host key in use
dsa_key.why: DSA keys are cryptographically broken and deprecated in OpenSSH 7.0+. The algorithm offers only 1024-bit security and is vulnerable to attacks when the random number generator produces weak values.
dsa_key.how:
1. Remove the DSA host key:
   sudo rm /etc/ssh/ssh_host_dsa_key*
2. Regenerate all host keys:
   sudo ssh-keygen -A
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh
4. Remove old fingerprints from clients:
   ssh-keygen -R <hostname>

no_passphrase.title: Private key without passphrase
no_passphrase.why: If the key file is copied or stolen — via a compromised server, backup leak, or misconfigured storage — the attacker gains immediate access to every system that trusts it. No cracking required.
no_passphrase.how:
1. Add a passphrase to an existing key:
   ssh-keygen -p -f ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
2. Use ssh-agent to avoid re-entering the passphrase every session
3. For service accounts, use dedicated keys with restrictive authorized_keys options (command=, from=)

client_strict_host_no.title: StrictHostKeyChecking disabled in SSH client config
client_strict_host_no.why: Disabling host verification allows man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks: an attacker can silently intercept your SSH session and impersonate the server with no warning displayed.
client_strict_host_no.how:
1. Remove StrictHostKeyChecking no from ~/.ssh/config
2. Use the default: StrictHostKeyChecking ask (first connection prompts, subsequent connections verify)
3. To skip verification for one specific host only, use a Host block:
   Host jump-host.example.com
       StrictHostKeyChecking no

ignore_rhosts_disabled.title: IgnoreRhosts disabled — .rhosts files trusted
ignore_rhosts_disabled.why: .rhosts files allow passwordless login based on hostname alone. Hostnames can be spoofed, making this a trivial authentication bypass that has been obsolete for decades.
ignore_rhosts_disabled.how:
1. Enable IgnoreRhosts (the default):
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  IgnoreRhosts yes
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

host_based_auth.title: Host-based authentication enabled
host_based_auth.why: Host-based authentication trusts the identity of a remote host rather than a user credential. If the trusted host is compromised, attackers automatically gain access to this server without any further authentication.
host_based_auth.how:
1. Disable host-based authentication (the default):
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  HostbasedAuthentication no
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

strict_modes_disabled.title: SSH StrictModes disabled
strict_modes_disabled.why: Without StrictModes, sshd skips permission checks on ~/.ssh and key files. World-readable private keys or group-writable home directories are silently accepted, effectively nullifying file permission security.
strict_modes_disabled.how:
1. Enable StrictModes (the default):
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  StrictModes yes
2. Fix file permissions:
   chmod 700 ~/.ssh
   chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

max_auth_tries.title: Too many authentication attempts allowed (MaxAuthTries > 3)
max_auth_tries.why: Each failed SSH attempt can probe valid usernames and test credentials. With the default of 6 attempts, an automated attack can test many passwords per connection before being disconnected. Reducing to 3 limits the credential surface per connection and makes brute-force campaigns significantly slower.
max_auth_tries.how:
1. Reduce MaxAuthTries:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  MaxAuthTries 3
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

permit_user_env.title: User environment variables allowed (PermitUserEnvironment yes)
permit_user_env.why: Allowing users to set environment variables via ~/.ssh/environment or authorized_keys options enables privilege escalation through environment manipulation: LD_PRELOAD, PATH, or PYTHONPATH overrides can redirect execution to attacker-controlled code even when the binary is trusted.
permit_user_env.how:
1. Disable user environment:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PermitUserEnvironment no
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

weak_ciphers.title: Weak SSH cipher suites in use
weak_ciphers.why: Legacy ciphers (3DES-CBC, arcfour/RC4, blowfish-CBC, CBC-mode AES) are cryptographically weak or broken. CBC-mode ciphers are vulnerable to BEAST and Lucky13 attacks. RC4 has statistical biases exploitable with enough traffic. An attacker recording sessions could later decrypt them.
weak_ciphers.how:
1. Restrict to strong ciphers:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
   Ciphers chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com,aes256-gcm@openssh.com,aes128-gcm@openssh.com,aes256-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes128-ctr
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh
3. Test your client still connects:
   ssh -Q cipher  # lists supported ciphers

weak_macs.title: Weak SSH MAC algorithms in use
weak_macs.why: Weak MACs (hmac-md5, hmac-sha1, umac-64) are vulnerable to collision attacks. A compromised MAC means message integrity cannot be guaranteed — an attacker in a man-in-the-middle position could tamper with session data in transit without detection. MD5 and SHA-1 are no longer collision-resistant.
weak_macs.how:
1. Restrict to strong MACs:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
   MACs hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com,hmac-sha2-256-etm@openssh.com,umac-128-etm@openssh.com
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

weak_kex.title: Weak SSH key exchange algorithms in use
weak_kex.why: Weak KEX algorithms (diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 uses a 1024-bit group; diffie-hellman-group14-sha1 uses deprecated SHA-1) offer insufficient forward secrecy. Nation-state actors have demonstrated precomputation attacks against standard 1024-bit DH groups (Logjam). Compromised KEX means the session key can be recovered after the fact.
weak_kex.how:
1. Restrict to strong KEX:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config
   KexAlgorithms curve25519-sha256,curve25519-sha256@libssh.org,diffie-hellman-group16-sha512,diffie-hellman-group18-sha512
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

rsa_weak.title: RSA host key too short (< 4096 bits)
rsa_weak.why: RSA keys shorter than 4096 bits are considered weak by modern cryptographic standards. As computing power increases and factorisation attacks improve, short keys become feasible to break. Keys under 2048 bits are practically broken today.
rsa_weak.how:
1. Generate a new 4096-bit RSA host key:
   sudo ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_rsa_key -N ''
2. Or prefer Ed25519 (shorter but stronger):
   sudo ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key -N ''
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh
4. Remove old host fingerprints on clients:
   ssh-keygen -R <hostname>

login_grace_time.title: LoginGraceTime too long (> 60s)
login_grace_time.why: A long grace period keeps unauthenticated TCP connections open for longer than necessary. An attacker can hold open many parallel SSH connections without completing authentication, potentially exhausting connection limits and degrading service for legitimate users.
login_grace_time.how:
1. Reduce LoginGraceTime:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  LoginGraceTime 30
2. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

no_allow_users.title: No AllowUsers / AllowGroups restriction in SSH config
no_allow_users.why: Without AllowUsers or AllowGroups, every system account with a valid credential can attempt SSH login — including service accounts, daemon users, and legacy accounts not intended for remote access. Restricting SSH to specific users dramatically reduces the attack surface.
no_allow_users.how:
1. Decide which users or groups need SSH access
2. Add an AllowUsers directive:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  AllowUsers alice bob deploy
3. Or restrict by group:
   AllowGroups sshusers
   sudo addgroup sshusers && sudo adduser alice sshusers
4. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

private_key_perms.title: SSH private key file permissions too open
private_key_perms.why: Private keys must be readable only by their owner (mode 0600). If group- or world-readable, any user sharing the same group — or any user on the system — can read the key and impersonate whoever owns it on every server that trusts it.
private_key_perms.how:
1. Restrict permissions:
   chmod 600 <key_path>
2. Verify ownership:
   ls -la <key_path>  →  -rw------- owner owner
3. For root-owned host keys:
   sudo chmod 600 /etc/ssh/ssh_host_*_key

authorized_keys_perms.title: authorized_keys file permissions too open
authorized_keys_perms.why: An authorized_keys file writable by others allows any user who can write to it to inject their own public key and gain SSH access as this account. Read access by others leaks information about who is authorised and from which hosts.
authorized_keys_perms.how:
1. Restrict permissions:
   chmod 600 ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
2. Verify ownership matches the account:
   ls -la ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
3. Enable StrictModes in sshd_config to enforce permission checks automatically:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  StrictModes yes

authorized_keys_dsa.title: DSA key in authorized_keys
authorized_keys_dsa.why: DSA keys use a cryptographically broken algorithm, deprecated in OpenSSH 7.0+. They offer only 1024-bit security and authentication via a DSA key provides weaker guarantees than any modern alternative.
authorized_keys_dsa.how:
1. Identify the DSA key line (starts with 'ssh-dss')
2. Remove it from ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
3. Ask the key owner to generate a new key:
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519
4. Add the new public key to authorized_keys
5. Confirm removal:
   grep 'ssh-dss' ~/.ssh/authorized_keys  # should return nothing

authorized_keys_weak_key.title: Weak RSA key in authorized_keys (< 4096 bits)
authorized_keys_weak_key.why: Short RSA keys in authorized_keys are as dangerous as weak host keys: an attacker who factors the private key gains permanent backdoor access to this account on every server that trusts it — including this one.
authorized_keys_weak_key.how:
1. Identify weak RSA keys (ssh-rsa entries with a short modulus)
2. Ask the key owner to generate a stronger key:
   ssh-keygen -t ed25519  # or: ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096
3. Replace the weak entry in authorized_keys with the new public key
4. Revoke the old key from all servers it was used on

authorized_keys_no_restrictions.title: authorized_keys entries without command or host restrictions
authorized_keys_no_restrictions.why: authorized_keys supports options (command=, from=, restrict) that limit what a key can do and from where. Without restrictions, a compromised key grants unrestricted shell access from any IP. For service or deployment keys this violates the principle of least privilege.
authorized_keys_no_restrictions.how:
1. For service keys, add a command= restriction:
   command="/usr/bin/rsync --server ...",no-pty,no-agent-forwarding ssh-ed25519 AAAA...
2. For keys from known sources, add a from= restriction:
   from="192.168.1.0/24" ssh-ed25519 AAAA...
3. Use the restrict option to disable all optional features:
   restrict,command="..." ssh-ed25519 AAAA...

authorized_keys_duplicate.title: Duplicate entries in authorized_keys
authorized_keys_duplicate.why: Duplicate keys suggest the file was modified without proper housekeeping — potentially by automation or by a user who lost track of what was added. Stale duplicates may belong to revoked users or compromised credentials that were never cleaned up.
authorized_keys_duplicate.how:
1. De-duplicate authorized_keys:
   sort -u ~/.ssh/authorized_keys > /tmp/ak_clean && mv /tmp/ak_clean ~/.ssh/authorized_keys
2. Review each key comment to verify it belongs to an active, authorised user
3. Remove any key whose owner is no longer authorised

dir_perms.title: ~/.ssh directory permissions too open
dir_perms.why: The ~/.ssh directory must be mode 0700 (owner only). If group- or world-readable, any user on the system can enumerate authorized_keys, known_hosts, and discover which systems this account can access. If writable, they can inject their own public key.
dir_perms.how:
1. Fix directory permissions:
   chmod 700 ~/.ssh
2. Fix all files inside:
   chmod 600 ~/.ssh/*
   chmod 644 ~/.ssh/*.pub 2>/dev/null; true
3. Verify:
   ls -la ~ | grep .ssh  →  drwx------

client_forward_agent.title: SSH agent forwarding enabled in client config (ForwardAgent yes)
client_forward_agent.why: Agent forwarding passes your SSH authentication credentials through to the remote server. If that server is compromised, root on that server can use your agent to authenticate as you on any other server your key grants access to — without ever seeing your private key.
client_forward_agent.how:
1. Disable agent forwarding globally:
   nano ~/.ssh/config  →  ForwardAgent no
2. Enable it only for specific trusted jump hosts where strictly necessary:
   Host jump.trusted.example.com
       ForwardAgent yes
3. Prefer ProxyJump for chaining SSH connections instead of agent forwarding

client_known_hosts_devnull.title: SSH client known_hosts pointed to /dev/null
client_known_hosts_devnull.why: Pointing known_hosts to /dev/null disables host key verification entirely. Every SSH connection silently accepts any host key — including a man-in-the-middle attacker presenting a forged key. This is equivalent to never verifying server identity.
client_known_hosts_devnull.how:
1. Remove the UserKnownHostsFile /dev/null line from ~/.ssh/config
2. Let SSH use its default: ~/.ssh/known_hosts
3. On first connection to each host, verify the fingerprint out-of-band before accepting it

known_hosts_deprecated.title: Deprecated key type in known_hosts
known_hosts_deprecated.why: Entries in known_hosts using deprecated algorithms (DSA, short RSA) provide weak integrity guarantees for host verification. If an attacker can forge a key of that type, they can impersonate the target host without triggering a warning.
known_hosts_deprecated.how:
1. Remove the deprecated entry:
   ssh-keygen -R <hostname>
2. Reconnect to the server — SSH will re-add it with its current key type
3. Ask the server admin to ensure only Ed25519 or RSA-4096 host keys are active

known_hosts_duplicate.title: Duplicate entries in known_hosts
known_hosts_duplicate.why: Multiple entries for the same host with different keys can cause confusion and may allow SSH to silently accept a stale or compromised key. It also indicates the file has not been maintained.
known_hosts_duplicate.how:
1. Remove all entries for the affected host:
   ssh-keygen -R <hostname>
2. Reconnect to add a single clean entry
3. Periodically clean known_hosts of stale entries for decommissioned hosts

world_writable.title: World-writable sensitive file
world_writable.why: Any local user on the system can modify this file. For configuration files (sshd_config, sudoers) this allows privilege escalation. For credential files it allows tampering that persists across sessions.
world_writable.how:
1. Identify the file and owner:
   ls -la <path>
2. Remove world-write permission:
   sudo chmod o-w <path>
3. Verify the fix:
   ls -la <path>  →  last three bits should be ---

too_permissive.title: File permissions too open
too_permissive.why: Overly permissive files can be read or written by unintended users. SSH keys readable by others allow impersonation. Configuration files readable by all may leak credentials or internal paths.
too_permissive.how:
1. Note the expected permissions shown in the audit output
2. Apply the correct permissions:
   sudo chmod <expected> <path>
3. Verify:
   ls -la <path>

sudoers_nopasswd_all.title: NOPASSWD:ALL in sudoers (unrestricted passwordless sudo)
sudoers_nopasswd_all.why: Grants full, unrestricted root access without any password. If this account is compromised — malware, stolen session token, weak password — the attacker has immediate full system control with zero additional effort.
sudoers_nopasswd_all.how:
1. Edit sudoers safely:
   sudo visudo
2. Replace NOPASSWD:ALL with a specific command list, e.g.:
   user ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/apt-get
3. If passwordless sudo is needed for automation, isolate it to a dedicated service account with a minimal allowed command list

ssh_host_key_perms.title: SSH host key permissions too open
ssh_host_key_perms.why: SSH host private keys must be readable only by root. If a non-root user can read the host key, they can impersonate this server to any client — enabling a man-in-the-middle attack on future SSH connections.
ssh_host_key_perms.how:
1. Restrict permissions:
   sudo chmod 600 <path>
2. Verify root ownership:
   sudo chown root:root <path>
3. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

security_pending.title: Security updates pending
security_pending.why: Pending security updates mean the system contains known vulnerabilities with public CVEs and often public exploits. Attackers actively scan for unpatched systems. Every day of delay increases the window of exposure.
security_pending.how:
1. Apply security updates now:
   sudo apt-get upgrade
2. Preview what would be applied:
   sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run
3. Apply only security patches automatically:
   sudo unattended-upgrade
4. If kernel updates are included, reboot:
   sudo reboot

server.why: Pending security updates on a server create known, exploitable vulnerabilities. Attackers prioritise recently-published CVEs where patches exist but have not been applied — this is the most common attack vector on public-facing servers. Apply updates immediately.

desktop.why: Pending security updates affect all profiles, but on a desktop the most critical are kernel, browser, and library updates that handle untrusted input. Apply them promptly to protect against local privilege escalation and drive-by attack vectors.

container.why: In a container, pending updates should be addressed by rebuilding the image from an updated base rather than running apt inside the container. Running apt upgrade in a running container is a temporary workaround — the correct solution is updating your Dockerfile base image and redeploying.
container.how:
Rebuild from an updated base image:
   # Update your Dockerfile's FROM tag or use --pull to get the latest:
   docker build --pull -t <your-image> .
   docker compose up -d
For an immediate stop-gap only:
   docker exec -it <container> apt-get update && apt-get upgrade -y

unattended_not_configured.title: Automatic security updates not configured
unattended_not_configured.why: Without automatic updates, security patches accumulate until someone manually applies them. Maintenance windows of exposure grow over time, and critical patches are often missed on servers without active monitoring.
unattended_not_configured.how:
1. Install the package:
   sudo apt install unattended-upgrades
2. Configure it interactively:
   sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades
3. Verify the service is active:
   sudo systemctl status unattended-upgrades
4. Test with a dry run:
   sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run -d

server.why: On an exposed server, every unpatched day is an open window. Attackers actively scan for systems missing recent CVEs. Manual update management on a server almost always means patches lag — automatic security updates are non-negotiable on public-facing infrastructure.

desktop.why: On a desktop, manual update management is common and acceptable. The risk is lower since no inbound services are publicly exposed. However, delaying security patches for more than a week increases local privilege escalation and browser/library exploit risk.

container.why: In a container environment, updates are managed at the image level — not via unattended-upgrades. If your pipeline regularly rebuilds from an updated base image, this finding does not apply. Verify your CI/CD includes base image refresh.
container.how:
Rebuild the image from an updated base rather than running apt inside the container:
   # Update your Dockerfile base image tag, then:
   docker build --pull -t <your-image> .
   docker compose up -d
For the host system (if unattended-upgrades is needed there):
   sudo apt install unattended-upgrades
   sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades

rp_filter_disabled.title: Reverse path filtering disabled (rp_filter = 0)
rp_filter_disabled.why: Without reverse path filtering, the kernel accepts packets from source IP addresses that could not have arrived via the receiving interface — a sign of IP spoofing. This enables spoofed-source attacks and can be used to bypass firewall rules that rely on source IP.
rp_filter_disabled.how:
1. Enable immediately (takes effect now):
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1
2. Make it permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-rp-filter.conf
3. Apply all sysctl settings:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: On a public-facing server, reverse path filtering is a fundamental network hardening measure. Without it, an attacker can send packets with a forged source IP, potentially bypassing IP-based access controls or enabling amplification attacks. The fix is zero-cost and has no functional side effects on standard infrastructure.

desktop.why: On a desktop, reverse path filtering provides defence-in-depth. The practical risk is lower since no public inbound services are exposed, but enabling it costs nothing and eliminates a class of IP spoofing attacks on local network traffic.

container.why: In a container, sysctl network settings are controlled by the host kernel. This setting cannot be changed from within a standard container. Apply the fix on the host system.
container.how:
Apply on the host system (not inside the container):
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-rp-filter.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

redirects_enabled.title: ICMP redirects accepted (accept_redirects = 1)
redirects_enabled.why: ICMP redirect messages can instruct the kernel to change its routing tables. An attacker on the local network can send forged ICMP redirects to reroute traffic through a machine they control, enabling a routing hijack or man-in-the-middle attack.
redirects_enabled.how:
1. Disable immediately (takes effect now):
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0
2. Make it permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-redirects.conf
3. Apply all sysctl settings:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: ICMP redirects can be used by an attacker on the local network to poison a server's routing table, redirecting its traffic through a malicious gateway (MITM). On a server, accepting ICMP redirects should never be enabled — there is no legitimate use case on standard infrastructure.

desktop.why: ICMP redirect acceptance is a minor risk on a desktop, primarily relevant on untrusted networks (public Wi-Fi, corporate LANs). Disabling it is a good practice with no functional impact for typical desktop users.

container.why: ICMP redirect settings are kernel-level and controlled by the host. This finding is not actionable from within a container. Verify and fix on the host system.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-redirects.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

log_martians_disabled.title: Martian packet logging disabled (log_martians = 0)
log_martians_disabled.why: Martian packets have source addresses that are impossible given the routing table — a strong indicator of IP spoofing, forged packets, or scanning. Without logging them, early-stage reconnaissance and spoofing attacks leave no trace. Enabling this logging is low-cost and provides valuable forensic data.
log_martians_disabled.how:
1. Enable immediately:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians=1
2. Make it permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-security.conf
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians=1' | sudo tee >> /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-security.conf
3. Apply:
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: Logging martian packets on a server is essential for detecting IP spoofing and network reconnaissance. Without it, early-stage scanning and spoofing attacks leave no trace in logs, making incident investigation much harder.

desktop.why: Martian packet logging is a useful forensic tool but generates noise on busy home networks. It is a low-priority hardening item on a desktop — enable it if you want visibility into anomalous local network traffic.

container.why: Sysctl logging settings are host-level and not configurable from within a standard container. This finding is not actionable in a container context. Address it on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians=1
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-security.conf
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-security.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

rp_filter_loose.title: Reverse path filtering in loose mode (rp_filter = 2)
rp_filter_loose.why: Loose mode (rp_filter=2) accepts packets as long as any route to the source exists, not necessarily via the receiving interface. This provides weaker protection than strict mode (=1) against IP spoofing and source-routing attacks. Strict mode drops packets whose reverse path does not match the interface they arrived on.
rp_filter_loose.how:
1. Switch to strict mode:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1
2. Make it permanent:
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-rp-filter.conf
3. Apply:
   sudo sysctl --system
Note: strict mode may break asymmetric routing (e.g. multi-homed servers). Verify network connectivity after applying.

server.why: Loose mode (rp_filter=2) provides weaker protection than strict mode (=1) on a server. On a single-interface server, strict mode should be preferred as it rejects more spoofed packets. Loose mode is only justified on multi-homed servers with asymmetric routing.

desktop.why: On a single-interface desktop, loose mode offers little protection compared to strict mode. Strict mode (=1) is safe and recommended unless you have specific asymmetric routing requirements, which are uncommon on desktops.

container.why: Same as rp_filter_disabled — this is a host kernel setting that cannot be modified from within a standard container. Apply on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1
   echo 'net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1' | sudo tee -a /etc/sysctl.d/99-rp-filter.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

risky_fs.title: Risky filesystem kernel modules loaded
risky_fs.why: Filesystem drivers (cramfs, freevxfs, hfs, hfsplus, jffs2, squashfs, udf, usb_storage) expand kernel attack surface unnecessarily on servers. Vulnerabilities in these drivers can be triggered by mounting a maliciously crafted filesystem image or inserting a USB device, potentially enabling privilege escalation or arbitrary code execution in kernel space.
risky_fs.how:
1. Unload the module now:
   sudo modprobe -r <module_name>
2. Blacklist to prevent reloading:
   echo 'blacklist <module>' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-fs.conf
   echo 'install <module> /bin/false' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-fs.conf
3. Rebuild initramfs:
   sudo update-initramfs -u
Note: only blacklist modules your system does not use (e.g. usb_storage is needed for USB drives).

server.why: Exotic filesystem modules (cramfs, freevxfs, hfs, hfsplus, jffs2, squashfs, udf) expand kernel attack surface on a server. Vulnerabilities in these drivers can be triggered by a crafted filesystem image, potentially enabling kernel-space privilege escalation. Blacklist what you do not use.

desktop.why: Most of these filesystems are not needed on a typical desktop. However, if you mount removable media with unusual filesystems (e.g. HFS+ from a Mac drive, UDF from a DVD), blacklisting those specific modules would prevent mounting them. Evaluate which ones you actually need before blacklisting.

container.why: Kernel module loading is restricted by default in containers (CAP_SYS_MODULE not granted). This finding is not actionable from within a container — address it on the host system.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   echo 'blacklist <module>' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-fs.conf
   echo 'install <module> /bin/false' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-fs.conf
   sudo update-initramfs -u

risky_net.title: Risky network protocol kernel modules loaded
risky_net.why: Protocols like DCCP, SCTP, RDS, and TIPC have had critical kernel vulnerabilities (CVEs with remote code execution and privilege escalation). These protocols are rarely needed on standard servers and represent unnecessary kernel attack surface. Loading them makes the system exploitable by sending crafted network packets to any open socket.
risky_net.how:
1. Unload the module now:
   sudo modprobe -r <module_name>
2. Blacklist to prevent reloading:
   echo 'blacklist <module>' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-net.conf
   echo 'install <module> /bin/false' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-net.conf
3. Rebuild initramfs:
   sudo update-initramfs -u
Note: SCTP is used by some telephony and clustering software. Verify before blacklisting.

server.why: Protocols DCCP, SCTP, RDS, and TIPC have had critical kernel CVEs with remote code execution and privilege escalation. These protocols are essentially never used on standard servers. Their presence in the running kernel means a crafted network packet could trigger a known kernel vulnerability.

desktop.why: These network protocols are almost never used on a desktop. Blacklisting them has no practical impact on desktop networking and closes a class of historical kernel vulnerabilities.

container.why: Kernel module loading is restricted in containers. This finding is not actionable from within a container — address it on the host.
container.how:
Apply on the host system:
   echo 'blacklist <module>' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-net.conf
   echo 'install <module> /bin/false' | sudo tee -a /etc/modprobe.d/blacklist-rare-net.conf
   sudo update-initramfs -u

pipe_to_shell.title: Pipe-to-shell pattern in system cron (curl/wget | sh)
pipe_to_shell.why: Fetching a script and piping it directly to a shell bypasses all integrity checks. If the remote server is compromised, the DNS is hijacked, or the connection is intercepted (plain HTTP), arbitrary code runs with the cron job's privileges — often root. There is no way to audit or version-control what will be executed at runtime.
pipe_to_shell.how:
1. Identify the cron entry in /etc/cron.* or /etc/crontab
2. Replace with a two-step approach:
   a. Download to a file: curl -fsSL -o /tmp/script.sh https://...
   b. Verify checksum: sha256sum -c /tmp/script.sha256
   c. Execute: bash /tmp/script.sh
3. Better: host the script locally, pin it in version control,
   and reference the local copy from cron

world_writable.title: World-writable script referenced in system cron
world_writable.why: Any local user can modify a world-writable script. Because cron runs it on a schedule — often as root — overwriting the script is a trivial local privilege escalation: no exploit needed, just write access to the file. This is a classic persistence and escalation technique.
world_writable.how:
1. Remove world-write permission:
   sudo chmod o-w <path>
2. Verify ownership is correct (should be root):
   ls -la <path>
3. Review the script content for unexpected modifications:
   sudo cat <path>

enabled_inactive.title: Security service enabled at boot but currently inactive
enabled_inactive.why: A service configured to start at boot but currently stopped may have crashed, been misconfigured, or been deliberately disabled. If the service is a security control (firewall, intrusion detection, log daemon), its absence creates a window during which threats go undetected or unblocked. The system appears protected at startup but is not at runtime.
enabled_inactive.how:
1. Check why the service stopped:
   sudo journalctl -u <service> -n 50
2. Restart and verify:
   sudo systemctl start <service>
   sudo systemctl status <service>
3. If the service crashes on start, investigate the config:
   sudo systemctl status <service> --no-pager -l
4. Ensure it remains enabled:
   sudo systemctl enable <service>

server.why: A service enabled at boot but currently inactive on a server may indicate a crashed or misconfigured security control. It will restart at next boot, potentially exposing a port that appears closed right now. On a server, investigate and resolve immediately.

desktop.why: On a desktop, an enabled-but-inactive service is typically a leftover from an old installation. While the risk is lower (no inbound exposure expected), it wastes startup time and may cause subtle issues. Disable unused services as a hygiene measure.

container.why: In a container, systemd is often not the init system. If your container uses a lightweight init (s6, runit, supervisord), this finding may not apply. If systemd is present in the container, follow the server guidance.

duplicate_found.title: Duplicate or redundant UFW rules
duplicate_found.why: Duplicate firewall rules do not improve security but add confusion and maintenance overhead. Redundant rules make the policy harder to audit and can cause unexpected behaviour when rules are later modified or deleted, since UFW processes rules in order.
duplicate_found.how:
1. List rules with numbers:
   sudo ufw status numbered
2. Identify and delete the redundant rule:
   sudo ufw delete <number>
3. Verify the remaining ruleset:
   sudo ufw status verbose

open_any_found.title: Open wildcard rule (ALLOW from Anywhere to Anywhere)
open_any_found.why: A rule allowing all traffic from anywhere to anywhere negates the entire firewall for the affected port or protocol. This is equivalent to having no firewall at all — any external host can reach any open service.
open_any_found.how:
1. Identify the wildcard rule:
   sudo ufw status numbered
2. Delete it:
   sudo ufw delete <number>
3. Replace with specific rules covering only the required sources and ports:
   sudo ufw allow from 192.168.1.0/24 to any port 22
4. Confirm the default policy is deny:
   sudo ufw default deny incoming

ipv6_missing.title: IPv4 rules present but no equivalent IPv6 rules
ipv6_missing.why: If a service is reachable over both IPv4 and IPv6 but only IPv4 is covered, the IPv6 path is completely unfiltered. An attacker using IPv6 bypasses all the firewall rules that appear to protect the service. This asymmetry is a common blind spot.
ipv6_missing.how:
1. Ensure /etc/default/ufw has IPV6=yes
2. UFW rules added without specifying a protocol apply to both IPv4 and IPv6 automatically:
   sudo ufw allow 22/tcp  # creates both v4 and v6 rules
3. Check which services listen on IPv6:
   sudo ss -tlnp | grep ':::'
4. Reload UFW:
   sudo ufw reload

ufw_disabled_listeners_present.title: Services listening on IPv6 but UFW IPv6 support is disabled
ufw_disabled_listeners_present.why: With UFW IPv6 disabled (IPV6=no in /etc/default/ufw), no ip6tables rules are loaded. Any service listening on a dual-stack address (::) is reachable from the network over IPv6 without any firewall filtering, regardless of what UFW shows for IPv4.
ufw_disabled_listeners_present.how:
1. Enable UFW IPv6 support:
   sudo nano /etc/default/ufw  →  IPV6=yes
2. Reload UFW to apply ip6tables rules:
   sudo ufw reload
3. Verify ip6tables rules are now active:
   sudo ip6tables -L INPUT -n | head -20

server.why: If UFW IPv6 support is disabled (IPV6=no) but services listen on IPv6 addresses, those ports are completely unmanaged by UFW. All IPv6 inbound traffic reaches the service without any filtering. On a server, this is a significant firewall gap that must be corrected.

desktop.why: On a desktop, this finding is informational. Most services listening on IPv6 are bound to loopback (::1) or link-local addresses (fe80::) with no external reachability. Enable UFW IPv6 support as best practice, but the immediate risk is low.

container.why: IPv6 management in containers is handled by the host network stack. This finding is typically not actionable from within a container. Check the host UFW configuration.

port_no_v6_rule.title: Service listening on IPv6 without a UFW IPv6 rule
port_no_v6_rule.why: A service bound to an IPv6 address with no corresponding UFW rule relies only on the default policy. If the default policy is permissive or unset, the service is reachable from any IPv6 source with no filtering. Firewall policies should be explicit for all listening addresses.
port_no_v6_rule.how:
1. Identify which service is listening:
   sudo ss -tlnp | grep ':::'
2. Add an explicit UFW rule (applies to both IPv4 and IPv6 by default):
   sudo ufw allow <port>/tcp
3. Or deny it explicitly if the service should not be reachable:
   sudo ufw deny <port>/tcp
4. Reload:
   sudo ufw reload

server.why: A service listening on IPv6 without an explicit UFW rule is accessible via IPv6 but unfiltered. On a server with a public IPv6 address, this creates an uncontrolled exposure path that bypasses all your IPv4 firewall rules. Add explicit rules for every listening port.

desktop.why: On a desktop, most IPv6 exposure is local. The risk depends on whether you have a public routable IPv6 address (a /64 from your ISP). On typical home networks using NAT or link-local only, this is informational — but adding explicit UFW rules is still good practice.

container.why: IPv6 connectivity in containers depends on the host network configuration and container runtime. If containers are not externally reachable via IPv6, this finding is informational. Check your container network setup before adding rules.

ufw_enabled_kernel_disabled.title: UFW IPv6 enabled but kernel IPv6 support is disabled
ufw_enabled_kernel_disabled.why: If UFW is configured to manage IPv6 (IPV6=yes) but the kernel has IPv6 disabled (net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=1), the intended ip6tables rules are silently never loaded. The system has an inconsistent configuration that may give a false sense of IPv6 protection.
ufw_enabled_kernel_disabled.how:
1. Option A — enable IPv6 in the kernel:
   sudo sysctl -w net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=0
   echo 'net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6=0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipv6.conf
   sudo sysctl --system
2. Option B — disable UFW IPv6 to match the kernel setting:
   sudo nano /etc/default/ufw  →  IPV6=no
   sudo ufw reload

no_quality_module.title: No password quality module configured (pam_pwquality / pam_cracklib)
no_quality_module.why: Without a PAM quality module, the system imposes no complexity requirements on local passwords. Users can set trivially guessable passwords (dictionary words, 'password123', single characters) that are trivial to crack offline if /etc/shadow is ever leaked.
no_quality_module.how:
1. Install pam_pwquality:
   sudo apt install libpam-pwquality
2. Configure minimum requirements in /etc/security/pwquality.conf:
   minlen = 12
   dcredit = -1
   ucredit = -1
   lcredit = -1
   ocredit = -1
3. Verify PAM includes pwquality:
   grep pam_pwquality /etc/pam.d/common-password

weak_minlen.title: Minimum password length too short (< 8 characters)
weak_minlen.why: Short passwords dramatically reduce the search space for offline brute-force and dictionary attacks. A 6-character password with common character sets can be fully cracked in minutes with modern hardware. NIST SP 800-63B recommends at least 8 characters; CIS recommends 14.
weak_minlen.how:
1. Increase minlen in /etc/security/pwquality.conf:
   sudo nano /etc/security/pwquality.conf  →  minlen = 12
2. Test the policy interactively:
   pwscore
3. Existing passwords are not affected — enforce a reset cycle for active accounts if compliance requires it

no_expiry.title: No password expiry policy configured
no_expiry.why: Without password expiry, compromised credentials remain valid indefinitely. If an attacker silently obtains a password (phishing, database leak, keylogger), they retain access until the user voluntarily changes it. Expiry forces periodic rotation and limits the exposure window.
no_expiry.how:
1. Set a global expiry policy in /etc/login.defs:
   PASS_MAX_DAYS 90
   PASS_MIN_DAYS 1
   PASS_WARN_AGE 14
2. Apply to existing accounts:
   sudo chage -M 90 <username>
3. Check current settings:
   sudo chage -l <username>
Note: NIST SP 800-63B now recommends long complex passwords without forced expiry. Adjust policy to your compliance requirements.

uid_zero.title: Non-root account with UID 0 detected
uid_zero.why: UID 0 is the superuser identifier. Any account with UID 0 has unrestricted root-equivalent access to the entire system — bypassing file permissions, sudo rules, and audit trails. A second UID-0 account is a common backdoor left by attackers or misconfigured systems. Only 'root' itself should ever hold UID 0.
uid_zero.how:
1. List all UID 0 accounts:
   awk -F: '($3 == 0) {print $1}' /etc/passwd
2. Lock or delete any non-root UID 0 account:
   sudo passwd -l <username>   # lock (preferred)
   sudo userdel <username>     # delete if no longer needed
3. Verify only root remains:
   awk -F: '($3 == 0) {print $1}' /etc/passwd  →  root

empty_password.title: Account with empty (blank) password detected
empty_password.why: An account without a password can be logged into by anyone without credentials — locally, over SSH (if PermitEmptyPasswords is on), or via su. Even with SSH key-only authentication, a single misconfiguration can open unauthenticated access. Empty passwords are never intentional in production.
empty_password.how:
1. List accounts with empty passwords:
   sudo awk -F: '($2 == "") {print $1}' /etc/shadow
2. Set a strong password immediately:
   sudo passwd <username>
3. If the account is a service account that should not be logged in:
   sudo passwd -l <username>   # lock it
4. Check SSH config: ensure PermitEmptyPasswords no in /etc/ssh/sshd_config

expired_account.title: User account with expired password detected
expired_account.why: Expired accounts may still be usable depending on PAM configuration and the value of INACTIVE in /etc/shadow. More importantly, they indicate accounts that are not actively maintained — forgotten accounts accumulate over time and represent a persistent attack surface if credentials are ever leaked.
expired_account.how:
1. List expired accounts:
   sudo chage -l <username>  →  check 'Password expired'
2. Renew the password if the account is active:
   sudo passwd <username>
3. Lock the account if it is no longer in use:
   sudo passwd -l <username>  # or: sudo usermod -e 1 <username>
4. Audit all accounts regularly:
   sudo chage --list <username> for each login user

no_shadow.title: /etc/shadow not readable — account security checks incomplete
no_shadow.why: /etc/shadow stores hashed passwords and account aging data. Without read access, bob cannot verify empty passwords, expiry policies, or UID 0 anomalies. This finding is informational only and means the audit is running without full privilege for account checks.
no_shadow.how:
1. This is not a configuration problem — run the full audit as root:
   sudo bob
2. Ensure /etc/shadow has correct permissions (640, root:shadow):
   sudo chmod 640 /etc/shadow
   sudo chown root:shadow /etc/shadow

smart_failed.title: SMART overall health check FAILED
smart_failed.why: A SMART health failure means the drive's own firmware predicts imminent failure. Data loss is likely imminent. This is the most critical disk warning — the drive should be considered unreliable immediately and replaced.
smart_failed.how:
1. Back up all data immediately — do not wait
2. Get the full SMART report:
   sudo smartctl -a <device>
3. Run a short self-test to confirm:
   sudo smartctl -t short <device>
   sudo smartctl -l selftest <device>  # after ~2 min
4. Replace the drive
5. Restore from backup to the replacement drive

reallocated_sectors.title: Reallocated sectors detected (SMART attribute 5)
reallocated_sectors.why: Reallocated sectors mean the drive has found areas that could not be written reliably and remapped them to spare sectors. A growing count indicates progressive failure — the drive is actively hiding bad areas and more may fail without warning.
reallocated_sectors.how:
1. Get the full SMART report to see the count and trend:
   sudo smartctl -a <device>
2. Run a long self-test:
   sudo smartctl -t long <device>
3. Monitor: if the count is growing over weeks, replace the drive
4. Ensure backups are current

pending_sectors.title: Current pending sectors detected (SMART attribute 197)
pending_sectors.why: Pending sectors are areas the drive has flagged for reallocation but has not yet remapped. They may already be unreadable. This is an active data-loss risk — files stored on these sectors may be unrecoverable.
pending_sectors.how:
1. Back up immediately — files on pending sectors may already be corrupt
2. Check full SMART data:
   sudo smartctl -a <device>
3. Run a filesystem check after unmounting to attempt repair:
   sudo fsck -f <device>
4. If the count persists or grows, replace the drive

uncorrectable_errors.title: Offline uncorrectable errors detected (SMART attribute 198)
uncorrectable_errors.why: Uncorrectable errors are sectors that could not be read even with multiple retries. Data in these sectors is permanently lost. Unlike pending sectors, these have already failed — there is no recovery without a prior backup.
uncorrectable_errors.how:
1. Back up immediately — data in affected sectors is permanently gone
2. Check the full SMART report:
   sudo smartctl -a <device>
3. Run a filesystem check:
   sudo fsck -f <device>  # when unmounted
4. Replace the drive — uncorrectable errors indicate physical media damage

partition_critical.title: Partition is critically full (≥ 90%)
partition_critical.why: A full partition causes service failures: databases crash, web servers return 500 errors, logs stop being written (masking security incidents), and processes needing temporary files fail unpredictably. At 100%, the system may become unresponsive.
partition_critical.how:
1. Find what is consuming space:
   du -sh <mountpoint>/* 2>/dev/null | sort -rh | head -20
2. Common culprits:
   - Logs: sudo journalctl --vacuum-size=500M
   - Old kernels: sudo apt autoremove
   - Docker: docker system prune
3. Move or delete large unnecessary files
4. If long-term, expand the partition or add storage

swappiness_ssd_wear.title: High swappiness on SSD — unnecessary write amplification
swappiness_ssd_wear.why: A high swappiness value causes the kernel to swap pages to disk aggressively even when RAM is available. On SSDs, each swap write counts against the drive's total write endurance (TBW). Sustained aggressive swapping shortens SSD lifespan, especially on entry-level drives.
swappiness_ssd_wear.how:
1. Check current value:
   cat /proc/sys/vm/swappiness
2. Set a lower value immediately:
   sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10  # workstation
   sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=1   # server
3. Make permanent:
   echo 'vm.swappiness=1' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

server.why: On a server with SSDs, high swappiness causes aggressive page swapping even when RAM is available, accelerating drive wear and increasing I/O latency. For database or I/O-intensive workloads, excessive swap activity can cause measurable performance degradation.

desktop.why: On a desktop with an SSD, high swappiness directly affects responsiveness and SSD longevity. The typical symptom is noticeable lag during memory-intensive tasks. Reducing swappiness to 10 is the standard recommendation for SSD desktops and has no downside.

container.why: Swappiness is a kernel-level setting controlled by the host. Container processes cannot modify vm.swappiness. This finding is not actionable inside a container — adjust vm.swappiness on the host system.
container.how:
Apply on the host system (not inside the container):
   sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10
   echo 'vm.swappiness=10' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

swappiness_unjustified.title: Swap in use despite abundant free RAM
swappiness_unjustified.why: The kernel is moving process memory to swap while RAM is largely available. This wastes swap write cycles (particularly damaging on SSDs), increases I/O latency for affected processes, and may indicate either a swappiness value that is too high for the workload or a memory leak in a running process.
swappiness_unjustified.how:
1. Identify processes with swapped-out memory:
   sudo smem -rs swap 2>/dev/null | head -15
2. Lower swappiness to reduce the tendency to swap:
   sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10
3. If a specific process is leaking memory, investigate:
   sudo top  # watch the RES/VIRT columns
4. Make swappiness permanent:
   echo 'vm.swappiness=10' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf

server.why: A server actively swapping while RAM is available indicates either a swappiness value too high for the workload or a memory-leaking process. Swap activity adds I/O latency and, on SSD-based servers, consumes write endurance. Investigate and tune.

desktop.why: On a desktop with sufficient RAM actively using swap, the first symptom is system sluggishness. Reducing swappiness from the default (60) to 10–20 improves responsiveness for typical desktop workloads without risking OOM events.

container.why: vm.swappiness cannot be tuned from within a container. If a container process is leaking memory, address the memory leak directly. For host-level swap tuning, apply the fix on the host.
container.how:
Investigate the memory-leaking process:
   docker stats <container>
For host-level swap tuning (apply on the host):
   sudo sysctl vm.swappiness=10
   echo 'vm.swappiness=10' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-swappiness.conf
   sudo sysctl --system

smb1_enabled.title: SMBv1 is enabled (EternalBlue / WannaCry vector)
smb1_enabled.why: SMBv1 is a 1990s protocol with multiple critical vulnerabilities. The NSA-developed EternalBlue exploit (leaked in 2017) targets SMBv1 and was used by WannaCry ransomware to infect over 200,000 systems in 150 countries in a single day. Microsoft deprecated SMBv1 in 2013. There is no legitimate reason to run SMBv1 today.
smb1_enabled.how:
1. Edit /etc/samba/smb.conf
2. In the [global] section add:
   min protocol = SMB2
3. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

null_passwords.title: Null passwords allowed (null passwords = yes)
null_passwords.why: Allows any account with no password set to authenticate to Samba with a blank password. An attacker only needs to know the username. Combined with guest or misconfigured accounts this grants immediate file system access with no credentials.
null_passwords.how:
1. Edit /etc/samba/smb.conf
2. In the [global] section set:
   null passwords = no
3. Ensure all accounts have passwords:
   sudo smbpasswd -a <user>
4. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

guest_writable.title: Guest-writable share (anonymous write access)
guest_writable.why: Any unauthenticated user on the network can upload, modify, or delete files in this share. This can be used to plant malware, exfiltrate data, or corrupt backups. Even on a trusted network, accidental or malicious modification without authentication creates serious integrity risks.
guest_writable.how:
1. Remove guest access entirely:
   [global] → map to guest = never
   [sharename] → remove 'guest ok = yes'
2. Or restrict to read-only:
   [sharename] → read only = yes
3. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

guest_readonly.title: Guest read-only share (anonymous read access)
guest_readonly.why: Any unauthenticated user on the network can read files from this share without providing credentials. While read-only access does not allow modification, it can be used for data exfiltration. Verify that all files in this share are intentionally public.
guest_readonly.how:
1. If anonymous access is not needed, remove guest access:
   [sharename] → remove 'guest ok = yes'
2. If read-only anonymous access is intentional, document it and ensure no sensitive data is in the share.
3. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

server_signing_disabled.title: Server signing disabled (NTLM relay attack vector)
server_signing_disabled.why: Without SMB signing, an attacker performing a man-in-the-middle attack can intercept and modify SMB traffic undetected, or relay NTLM authentication to other services. NTLM relay attacks are a standard technique in Active Directory penetration testing and real-world attacks (e.g. Responder, ntlmrelayx).
server_signing_disabled.how:
1. Edit /etc/samba/smb.conf
2. In the [global] section set:
   server signing = mandatory
3. Note: clients must also support signing (all modern clients do)
4. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

map_to_guest.title: map to guest = bad user (failed logins fall back to guest)
map_to_guest.why: When a user provides an invalid username, Samba silently logs them in as the guest account instead of returning an authentication error. This means an attacker who does not know a valid username still gets network access to all guest-accessible shares.
map_to_guest.how:
1. Edit /etc/samba/smb.conf
2. In the [global] section set:
   map to guest = never
3. Restart Samba:
   sudo systemctl restart smbd

db_very_outdated.title: Virus database critically outdated (> 30 days)
db_very_outdated.why: ClamAV's detection ability depends entirely on its signature database. An outdated database cannot detect malware discovered after the last update. Ransomware, trojans, and rootkits released in the past month would be completely invisible to the scanner.
db_very_outdated.how:
1. Update the database immediately:
   sudo freshclam
2. Enable automatic updates via the freshclam service:
   sudo systemctl enable --now clamav-freshclam
3. Verify cron or systemd timer is scheduling daily updates

server.why: An antivirus database older than 30 days on a server handling files (mail relay, upload service, shared storage) means recent malware strains are completely undetectable. Each day of delay adds hundreds of new undetectable signatures.

desktop.why: On a desktop, an outdated ClamAV database leaves you unprotected against recent malware. Since desktops handle user downloads, email attachments, and web content, keeping signatures current is essential for the tool to provide any meaningful protection.

container.why: ClamAV is rarely deployed in containers — scanning typically occurs at the host or gateway level, or via dedicated image scanners (Trivy, Snyk). If present, an outdated database in a container suggests the image rebuild cycle is not refreshing the database.

db_outdated.title: Virus database is outdated (> 7 days)
db_outdated.why: ClamAV releases new signature updates multiple times per day. After 7 days, hundreds of new malware signatures are missing from your database. This significantly reduces detection rates for recent threats.
db_outdated.how:
1. Update the database:
   sudo freshclam
2. Enable automatic daily updates:
   sudo systemctl enable --now clamav-freshclam
3. Check the freshclam timer:
   systemctl status clamav-freshclam

server.why: A ClamAV database 7–30 days old on a server is approaching the risk threshold. Automated freshclam updates should maintain the database without manual intervention — an outdated database suggests the automatic update process is failing.

desktop.why: On a desktop, a 7–30 day old database is a yellow flag. The freshclam daemon should handle updates automatically. If it is not running, re-enable it. Recent threats may be going undetected.

container.why: In a container, ClamAV database updates should be part of the image build pipeline. An outdated database in a running container indicates the image or update process needs review.

scan_very_old.title: Last scan is very old (> 90 days)
scan_very_old.why: Without regular scanning, infections can persist undetected for months. Linux systems are increasingly targeted by malware — web shells, crypto miners, backdoors, and rootkits do not announce themselves. Quarterly scans at minimum are needed to detect dormant infections.
scan_very_old.how:
1. Run an immediate scan of home directories:
   sudo clamscan -r /home --infected --log=/var/log/clamav/clamscan.log
2. Schedule weekly scans via cron:
   echo '0 2 * * 0 root clamscan -r /home --infected --log=/var/log/clamav/clamscan.log' | sudo tee /etc/cron.d/clamav-scan

server.why: If the last scan was over 90 days ago on a server handling files, malware may have been present for months. Web shells, crypto miners, and backdoors do not self-report. Run an immediate scan and establish regular weekly scans via cron.

desktop.why: A scan gap of 90+ days on a desktop means any malware received or downloaded during that period was not caught. Run an immediate scan and schedule weekly automated scans.

container.why: Periodic ClamAV scans inside containers are non-standard. Scanning typically occurs at the image build stage via tools like Trivy or Snyk. Manual ClamAV scans inside running containers are not a standard security practice in container pipelines.

scan_old.title: Last scan is over 30 days old
scan_old.why: Monthly scans leave a large window during which infections can establish persistence, exfiltrate data, or spread to other systems. On a server exposed to the internet, monthly scanning is insufficient.
scan_old.how:
1. Run a new scan:
   sudo clamscan -r /home --infected --log=/var/log/clamav/clamscan.log
2. Schedule weekly scans:
   echo '0 2 * * 0 root clamscan -r /home --infected --log=/var/log/clamav/clamscan.log' | sudo tee /etc/cron.d/clamav-scan

server.why: A 30–90 day scan gap on a server leaves a long window during which undetected malware could establish persistence. Increase scan frequency — weekly is the minimum recommended for production servers.

desktop.why: For a desktop, weekly scanning is a reasonable baseline. If it has been 30–90 days, re-enable the scheduled scan. Recent downloads or email attachments may have brought in undetected malware.

container.why: Same as scan_very_old — periodic ClamAV scans inside containers are non-standard. Focus on image security scanning (Trivy, Snyk) integrated into your CI/CD pipeline.

not_installed.title: Linux Audit Framework not installed
not_installed.why: auditd provides kernel-level logging of system calls, file access, authentication, and privileged commands. Without it, attackers can operate undetected — privilege escalations, unauthorized access, and sensitive file reads leave no forensic trace.
not_installed.how:
Install auditd and the dispatcher plugins:
  sudo apt install auditd audispd-plugins
  sudo systemctl enable --now auditd

Create a minimal rule set in /etc/audit/rules.d/99-local.rules:
  -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudoers

Load the rules:
  sudo augenrules --load

service_inactive.title: auditd installed but service not running
service_inactive.why: auditd is installed but stopped. Kernel events are not being logged in real time. Authentication events, sudo usage, and sensitive file access go unrecorded, eliminating forensic evidence if an incident occurs.
service_inactive.how:
Enable and start the service:
  sudo systemctl enable --now auditd

Verify it is running and rules are loaded:
  sudo systemctl status auditd
  sudo auditctl -l

no_rules.title: auditd running but no audit rules configured
no_rules.why: auditd is active but no rules are loaded. Only a minimal set of default events is captured. Critical events — access to /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, sudo invocations, privileged commands — go unlogged, making forensic analysis very difficult.
no_rules.how:
Create persistent rules in /etc/audit/rules.d/99-local.rules:
  -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudoers
  -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S execve -k commands

Reload rules:
  sudo augenrules --load
  sudo systemctl restart auditd

Verify:
  sudo auditctl -l

missing_sensitive_rules.title: Sensitive files not covered by audit rules
missing_sensitive_rules.why: Critical files such as /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, and /etc/sudoers are not monitored by auditd. Any unauthorized modification to these files could indicate privilege escalation or account takeover, and would leave no audit trail.
missing_sensitive_rules.how:
Add watch rules for the missing files in /etc/audit/rules.d/99-local.rules:
  -w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
  -w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudoers

Reload:
  sudo augenrules --load
  sudo systemctl restart auditd

server.why: On a server, unauthorized modifications to /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, or /etc/sudoers are high-severity indicators of privilege escalation or account takeover. Without watch rules for these files, such changes leave no audit trail — a critical gap for incident response and compliance.

desktop.why: Some sensitive files are not covered by auditd rules. On a desktop this is informational — these files are less frequently targeted — but adding watch rules provides an additional layer of forensic visibility.

setup_mode.title: Secure Boot is in Setup Mode (no Platform Key enrolled)
setup_mode.why: Secure Boot Setup Mode means no Platform Key is enrolled. Any bootloader, including a malicious one, can be loaded without verification. This effectively disables Secure Boot protections and allows persistent bootkits on systems with physical or early-boot access.
setup_mode.how:
Enroll your Platform Key via the UEFI firmware settings:
  1. Reboot and enter UEFI/BIOS (F2, F12, or Del).
  2. Navigate to Secure Boot → Key Management.
  3. Enroll a Platform Key (PK), Key Exchange Key (KEK), and database (db).

Alternatively, use mokutil to check state:
  mokutil --sb-state
  mokutil --enable-validation

disabled.title: Secure Boot is disabled
disabled.why: Secure Boot verifies that only trusted bootloaders and kernels load at startup. Without it, rootkits, bootkits, and malicious drivers can persist below the OS, bypassing all software-level defenses.
disabled.how:
Enable Secure Boot in your UEFI firmware settings:
  1. Reboot and enter UEFI/BIOS (F2, F12, or Del).
  2. Navigate to the Secure Boot settings.
  3. Set Secure Boot to Enabled.
  4. If you use custom kernels or third-party drivers, enroll a Machine Owner Key:
     sudo mokutil --import mok.der

server.why: Secure Boot is disabled. On servers this is common — cloud images, out-of-tree drivers (NVIDIA, ZFS), and custom kernels often require it to be disabled. This is noted for completeness; no score deduction is applied for server profiles.
server.how:
No action is required on server profiles. If you want to enable Secure Boot, ensure all loaded kernels and modules are signed, then enable it in UEFI settings. Use mokutil to enroll custom signing keys if needed:
  mokutil --sb-state
  mokutil --import mok.der

desktop.why: On a desktop, disabling Secure Boot allows rootkits, bootkits, and malicious drivers to load before the OS, bypassing all software-level defenses. This is a real threat vector for persistent, kernel-level attacks, especially on laptops or shared workstations.

not_installed.title: No file integrity monitoring tool installed
not_installed.why: Without a file integrity monitor (AIDE or Tripwire), there is no way to detect unauthorized modifications to system files, configuration files, or binaries. An attacker who gains access can replace binaries, add backdoors, or alter configuration without detection.
not_installed.how:
Install and initialize AIDE:
  sudo apt install aide
  sudo aideinit                    # creates the initial baseline database
  sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db

Schedule regular checks in cron:
  echo '0 3 * * * root /usr/bin/aide --check 2>&1 | mail -s "AIDE check" root' | sudo tee /etc/cron.d/aide-check

no_db.title: File integrity tool installed but no baseline database
no_db.why: The integrity monitoring tool is installed but no baseline database has been created. Without a baseline, the tool cannot detect changes to system files. Any modifications made before database initialization will never be flagged.
no_db.how:
Initialize the baseline database:
  For AIDE:     sudo aideinit && sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db
  For Tripwire: sudo tripwire --init

Then schedule regular checks:
  sudo crontab -e
  0 3 * * * /usr/bin/aide --check 2>&1 | mail -s 'AIDE report' root

no_check.title: Integrity baseline exists but no check has ever been run
no_check.why: A baseline database exists but no integrity check has been performed since initialization. Without regular checks, any file modification since baseline creation — including malicious ones — goes undetected.
no_check.how:
Run an integrity check immediately:
  For AIDE:     sudo aide --check
  For Tripwire: sudo tripwire --check

If the output shows unexpected changes, investigate each one. Schedule regular checks:
