  sudo crontab -e
  0 3 * * * /usr/bin/aide --check 2>&1 | mail -s 'AIDE report' root

check_old.title: File integrity check has not been run recently
check_old.why: The last file integrity check is outdated. Recent changes to system files — legitimate or malicious — have not been verified against the baseline. Integrity monitoring loses its value if checks are not performed regularly.
check_old.how:
Run a new integrity check:
  For AIDE:     sudo aide --check
  For Tripwire: sudo tripwire --check

Automate regular checks:
  sudo crontab -e
  0 3 * * * /usr/bin/aide --check 2>&1 | mail -s 'AIDE report' root

After verifying all known-good changes, update the baseline:
  sudo aide --update && sudo mv /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db

bypass_risk.title: Virtualisation bridge may bypass UFW FORWARD policy
bypass_risk.why: Hypervisors such as libvirt/KVM, VirtualBox, and VMware create Linux bridge interfaces (virbr0, vboxnet*, etc.) and inject their own iptables rules directly into the FORWARD chain. These rules can allow traffic between VMs and the host — or between VMs and the internet — independently of UFW's FORWARD policy. UFW manages only its own ruleset and cannot prevent bridge-injected rules from permitting forwarded traffic.
bypass_risk.how:
Audit the FORWARD rules inserted by the bridge:
  sudo iptables -L FORWARD -v --line-numbers | grep virbr0

This is expected behaviour for a VM host — review the output to confirm only legitimate VM traffic is forwarded.

To isolate VMs from the internet while keeping local host access, configure libvirt's network in isolated mode:
  virsh net-edit default  # set <forward mode='none'/> for isolated networks

If you no longer use virtual machines:
  sudo systemctl disable --now libvirtd

brute_force.title: Brute-force attacks detected in authentication logs
brute_force.why: Repeated failed login attempts indicate active automated attacks against this machine. If password authentication or weak credentials are in use, persistent brute-force campaigns will eventually succeed. Even with strong passwords, flood attacks consume CPU and lock out legitimate users.
brute_force.how:
1. Install and configure fail2ban:
   sudo apt install fail2ban
   sudo systemctl enable --now fail2ban
2. Verify the SSH jail is active:
   sudo fail2ban-client status sshd
3. Disable password authentication (use keys only):
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PasswordAuthentication no
4. Reduce MaxAuthTries:
   MaxAuthTries 3
5. Restart SSH:
   sudo systemctl restart ssh

public_login.title: Successful logins from public IP addresses detected
public_login.why: Remote logins from public IPs visible in auth logs confirm the machine is internet-reachable and actively accessed. Any credential compromise — brute force, stolen key, leaked password — would give an attacker an immediate shell on a live system.
public_login.how:
1. Restrict SSH access to known IPs via UFW:
   sudo ufw allow from <your-ip> to any port 22
   sudo ufw delete allow 22
2. Use key-only authentication:
   sudo nano /etc/ssh/sshd_config  →  PasswordAuthentication no
3. Review who is logging in:
   sudo last | head -20
4. Consider a VPN or port-knocking if remote access must be maintained

world_writable.title: Default umask allows world-writable file creation (umask 0000 or 0002)
world_writable.why: A world-writable umask means every new file created by any user is writable by all users on the system. Attackers with any local account can modify scripts, configs, and data files created by privileged processes — enabling privilege escalation and persistent backdoors.
world_writable.how:
1. Set a secure default umask in /etc/profile and /etc/bash.bashrc:
   umask 0022
2. For stricter environments:
   umask 0027
3. Verify the change takes effect:
   umask  # should return 0022 or stricter
4. Check /etc/login.defs:
   UMASK 022

group_writable.title: Default umask allows group-writable file creation (umask 002)
group_writable.why: A group-writable umask means every new file is writable by any member of the creating user's group. On multi-user systems or systems with shared service accounts, this can allow horizontal privilege escalation between users sharing a group.
group_writable.how:
1. Set umask to 0022 in /etc/profile:
   umask 0022
2. Verify:
   umask  # should return 0022

logging_off.title: UFW firewall logging is disabled
logging_off.why: Without firewall logs, blocked connection attempts, port scans, and intrusion attempts leave no trace. Forensic investigation after an incident becomes impossible — you cannot determine when an attack started, which ports were probed, or where traffic came from.
logging_off.how:
1. Enable UFW logging:
   sudo ufw logging on
2. For more detail:
   sudo ufw logging medium
   # or: sudo ufw logging high
3. Verify:
   sudo ufw status verbose | grep Logging
4. Logs appear in:
   /var/log/ufw.log  (or journald)

expired.title: TLS/SSL certificate has expired
expired.why: An expired certificate causes browsers and clients to display hard trust errors and refuse connections. Services may become completely inaccessible. Expired certificates are also a signal of poor certificate lifecycle management — attackers specifically look for expired certificates to exploit.
expired.how:
1. Identify which certificate is expired:
   sudo bob --check ssl_certs --verbose
2. For Let's Encrypt:
   sudo certbot renew --force-renewal
3. For manually managed certificates:
   openssl x509 -in /path/to/cert.pem -noout -dates
   Replace with a new certificate from your CA
4. Verify:
   openssl x509 -in /path/to/cert.pem -noout -enddate

expiring_critical.title: TLS/SSL certificate expires within 7 days
expiring_critical.why: A certificate expiring in under a week requires immediate action. Once expired, services stop working for all clients. Automated renewal may have failed silently — manual intervention is needed now to avoid an outage.
expiring_critical.how:
1. For Let's Encrypt:
   sudo certbot renew --force-renewal
   sudo systemctl reload nginx  # or apache2
2. Check renewal timer:
   sudo systemctl status certbot.timer
3. For manual certs, contact your CA immediately for a replacement
4. Verify the new expiry:
   openssl x509 -in /path/to/cert.pem -noout -enddate

expiring_soon.title: TLS/SSL certificate expires within 30 days
expiring_soon.why: Certificates expiring in under a month need attention before they expire. Automated renewal tools (certbot, acme.sh) should have already renewed them. A failure to renew automatically often indicates a misconfigured renewal job or DNS/port issue.
expiring_soon.how:
1. Force-renew Let's Encrypt certificates:
   sudo certbot renew
2. Check renewal logs:
   sudo journalctl -u certbot
3. Verify timer is active:
   sudo systemctl status certbot.timer
4. For manual certificates, request a renewal from your CA

pipe_to_shell.title: Systemd timer unit pipes downloaded content to a shell
pipe_to_shell.why: Piping curl or wget output directly to bash/sh executes arbitrary code from a remote server without any integrity verification. If the remote server is compromised, misconfigured, or the connection is intercepted, an attacker can execute any command as the user running the timer.
pipe_to_shell.how:
1. Identify the timer unit:
   sudo bob --check systemd_timers --verbose
2. Edit the unit to download first, verify, then execute:
   systemctl edit <unit>.service
3. Use checksums or package managers instead of curl-to-shell patterns
4. Consider using signed packages or configuration management tools

world_writable.title: Systemd timer ExecStart script is world-writable
world_writable.why: Any local user can modify a world-writable script that is executed by a privileged systemd timer. This is a direct privilege escalation path — write your code into the script and wait for the timer to fire as root.
world_writable.how:
1. Fix permissions on the script:
   sudo chmod 755 /path/to/script.sh
   sudo chown root:root /path/to/script.sh
2. Verify:
   ls -la /path/to/script.sh  # should show -rwxr-xr-x root root
3. Audit all timer scripts regularly:
   find /etc/systemd/system -name '*.service' | xargs grep -l ExecStart

user_created_root.title: User-created systemd timer runs as root
user_created_root.why: A non-package timer running as root that was created by a regular user is a strong indicator of a persistence mechanism or privilege escalation backdoor. Legitimate system services are installed by packages; user-created root timers are unusual and warrant immediate investigation.
user_created_root.how:
1. Identify and inspect the timer:
   systemctl list-timers --all
   systemctl cat <suspicious-timer>.service
2. Check who created the file:
   ls -la /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.service
3. If not a known legitimate service, disable and remove:
   sudo systemctl disable --now <unit>.timer
   sudo rm /etc/systemd/system/<unit>.*

fwupd_updates.title: Firmware updates available via fwupd
fwupd_updates.why: Firmware vulnerabilities (UEFI, NVMe, Thunderbolt, etc.) run below the operating system and cannot be patched by the OS. Unpatched firmware enables persistent rootkits that survive OS reinstallation, and can bypass Secure Boot, TPM attestation, and kernel mitigations.
fwupd_updates.how:
1. List available firmware updates:
   fwupdmgr get-updates
2. Apply updates:
   sudo fwupdmgr update
3. Reboot if required:
   sudo reboot
4. Automate future checks:
   sudo systemctl enable --now fwupd-refresh.timer

microcode_missing.title: CPU microcode update package not installed
microcode_missing.why: CPU microcode patches critical hardware vulnerabilities including Spectre, Meltdown, MDS, TAA, and many others. Without microcode updates, these side-channel attacks can allow unprivileged processes to read kernel memory, cross VM boundaries, and extract cryptographic keys.
microcode_missing.how:
1. Install the appropriate microcode package:
   # Intel CPU:
   sudo apt install intel-microcode
   # AMD CPU:
   sudo apt install amd64-microcode
2. Reboot to apply:
   sudo reboot
3. Verify microcode is loaded:
   grep microcode /proc/cpuinfo | head -1

privileged.title: Docker container running in privileged mode
privileged.why: A privileged container has full access to the host's devices and capabilities — it is effectively running as root on the host with all restrictions removed. Any process inside a privileged container can escape to the host, modify kernel parameters, mount host filesystems, and compromise the entire system.
privileged.how:
1. Identify the privileged container:
   docker ps --quiet | xargs docker inspect --format '{{.Name}} privileged={{.HostConfig.Privileged}}'
2. Remove the --privileged flag and grant only the specific capabilities needed:
   docker run --cap-add NET_ADMIN (instead of --privileged)
3. If the container genuinely needs privileged access, isolate it on a dedicated host
4. Use seccomp profiles and AppArmor policies

root_containers.title: Docker containers running as root (no user namespace remapping)
root_containers.why: Containers running as UID 0 inside the container map directly to root on the host when user namespace remapping is not configured. A container escape vulnerability — of which Docker has had several — gives an attacker immediate root on the host.
root_containers.how:
1. Add a non-root USER in your Dockerfile:
   USER 1000:1000
2. Or enable user namespace remapping globally:
   sudo nano /etc/docker/daemon.json
   { "userns-remap": "default" }
   sudo systemctl restart docker
3. Verify:
   docker run alpine id  # should not return uid=0

socket_mounted.title: Docker socket mounted inside a container
socket_mounted.why: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock into a container gives it full control of the Docker daemon — and therefore the host. From inside the container, an attacker can start a new privileged container, mount the host filesystem, and escape with a single docker command. This is a complete container isolation bypass.
socket_mounted.how:
1. Remove the socket mount from the container:
   Remove -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock from docker run
2. If the container needs to manage Docker (CI agents, Portainer), use:
   - Docker-in-Docker (dind) with explicit isolation
   - A Docker TCP socket with TLS authentication instead of the Unix socket
3. Audit running containers:
   docker ps -q | xargs docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}: {{.Mounts}}' | grep docker.sock

host_network.title: Docker container using host network mode
host_network.why: A container with --network=host shares the host's network namespace entirely. It can bind to any port on the host, listen on all interfaces, and access any network service running on localhost. Network-based container isolation does not exist for such containers.
host_network.how:
1. Remove --network=host and use explicit port publishing:
   docker run -p 8080:80 myimage  (instead of --network=host)
2. If host networking is required for performance (e.g. latency-sensitive apps), restrict capabilities and use AppArmor/seccomp profiles
3. Audit host-networked containers:
   docker ps -q | xargs docker inspect --format '{{.Name}}: {{.HostConfig.NetworkMode}}' | grep host

aslr_disabled.title: ASLR (Address Space Layout Randomisation) is disabled
aslr_disabled.why: ASLR randomises the memory address layout of processes, making it significantly harder to exploit memory corruption vulnerabilities (buffer overflows, use-after-free). Without ASLR, an attacker can predict the exact address of shellcode, ROP gadgets, and heap allocations, making exploits far more reliable.
aslr_disabled.how:
1. Enable ASLR permanently:
   sudo sysctl -w kernel.randomize_va_space=2
   echo 'kernel.randomize_va_space = 2' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-aslr.conf
2. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space  # should return 2

aslr_conservative.title: ASLR set to conservative mode (randomize_va_space=1)
aslr_conservative.why: Conservative ASLR (value 1) randomises stack and mmap() allocations but not the heap. Heap spray and heap-based exploitation techniques remain more reliable against a target with conservative ASLR than with full ASLR (value 2).
aslr_conservative.how:
1. Enable full ASLR:
   sudo sysctl -w kernel.randomize_va_space=2
   echo 'kernel.randomize_va_space = 2' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-aslr.conf
2. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space  # should return 2

ptrace_unrestricted.title: ptrace is unrestricted (kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=0)
ptrace_unrestricted.why: With unrestricted ptrace, any process can attach to and read/write the memory of any other process owned by the same user. An attacker with a low-privilege shell can extract credentials from browser sessions, SSH agents, gpg-agent, and sudo credential caches running in the same user session.
ptrace_unrestricted.how:
1. Restrict ptrace to parent processes only:
   sudo sysctl -w kernel.yama.ptrace_scope=1
   echo 'kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 1' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-ptrace.conf
2. For stricter environments (admins only):
   kernel.yama.ptrace_scope = 2
3. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/kernel/yama/ptrace_scope

dmesg_exposed.title: Kernel log (dmesg) accessible by unprivileged users
dmesg_exposed.why: The kernel ring buffer contains memory addresses, driver information, device names, and sometimes credentials passed as kernel parameters. Unprivileged access to dmesg significantly helps attackers defeat ASLR, identify kernel version and modules, and find attack surface.
dmesg_exposed.how:
1. Restrict dmesg to root:
   sudo sysctl -w kernel.dmesg_restrict=1
   echo 'kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-dmesg.conf
2. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/kernel/dmesg_restrict  # should return 1

kptr_exposed.title: Kernel pointer addresses exposed to unprivileged users (kptr_restrict=0)
kptr_exposed.why: Kernel pointer addresses in /proc/kallsyms, /proc/modules, and similar interfaces help attackers locate kernel code and data structures when attempting kernel exploitation. Exposing them makes bypassing kernel ASLR much easier.
kptr_exposed.how:
1. Restrict kernel pointer exposure:
   sudo sysctl -w kernel.kptr_restrict=2
   echo 'kernel.kptr_restrict = 2' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-kptr.conf
2. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/kernel/kptr_restrict  # should return 1 or 2

suid_dump_all.title: Core dumps enabled for SUID processes (fs.suid_dumpable=2)
suid_dump_all.why: When suid_dumpable is set to 2, SUID processes can produce core dumps readable by all users. Core dumps of SUID programs contain the full process memory — including any secrets, keys, or elevated-privilege data held in memory at crash time.
suid_dump_all.how:
1. Disable SUID core dumps:
   sudo sysctl -w fs.suid_dumpable=0
   echo 'fs.suid_dumpable = 0' | sudo tee /etc/sysctl.d/99-suid-dump.conf
2. Verify:
   cat /proc/sys/fs/suid_dumpable  # should return 0

unexpected_suid.title: Unexpected SUID binary detected
unexpected_suid.why: SUID (Set User ID) binaries execute with the file owner's privileges (typically root) regardless of who runs them. An unexpected SUID binary is either a privilege escalation backdoor planted by an attacker, or a legitimate tool left SUID unnecessarily. Either way, it represents an uncontrolled root execution path.
unexpected_suid.how:
1. Identify all SUID binaries:
   find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null
2. For each unexpected binary, investigate its origin:
   dpkg -S /path/to/binary
3. Remove the SUID bit if not required:
   sudo chmod u-s /path/to/binary
4. If the binary is unknown or suspicious:
   sha256sum /path/to/binary
   # Compare with known-good hash from the vendor

unexpected_sgid.title: Unexpected SGID binary detected
unexpected_sgid.why: SGID (Set Group ID) binaries execute with the file's group privileges. An unexpected SGID binary can provide access to privileged group resources (shadow, disk, docker, sudo) for any user who runs it — enabling group-level privilege escalation.
unexpected_sgid.how:
1. Identify all SGID binaries:
   find / -perm -2000 -type f 2>/dev/null
2. Investigate each unexpected binary:
   dpkg -S /path/to/binary
3. Remove the SGID bit if not required:
   sudo chmod g-s /path/to/binary

clamav.not_installed: ClamAV is not installed — no antivirus protection
clamav.not_installed_detail: ClamAV provides malware detection for files, shares, and email attachments. On Linux it is especially useful for scanning files shared with Windows users and for mail server integration (Postfix/Amavis).
clamav.freshclam_missing: freshclam is missing — virus database cannot be updated automatically
clamav.freshclam_missing_detail: freshclam downloads and keeps ClamAV’s virus signature database current. Without it, the database cannot be updated and the scanner gradually becomes blind to new threats.

clamav.db_not_found_detail: ClamAV is installed but no signature database was found in /var/lib/clamav/. Without signatures the scanner cannot detect any threat — it would report ‘no infections’ even on a fully compromised system.
clamav.db_very_outdated: Virus database is {days} day(s) old — critically outdated
clamav.db_very_outdated_detail: ClamAV publishes signature updates multiple times per day. After 30 days, thousands of new malware variants are completely invisible to the scanner. Ransomware, trojans, and rootkits discovered last month cannot be detected.
clamav.db_outdated: Virus database is {days} day(s) old — consider updating
clamav.db_outdated_detail: Virus signatures are released several times per day. After 7 days, hundreds of new variants are missing from the database, significantly reducing detection rates for recent threats.
clamav.db_ok: Virus database is up to date ({days} day(s) old)
clamav.clamd_inactive_detail: The clamav-daemon service enables on-access scanning and is required for integration with mail servers (Postfix, Amavis, etc.). Without the daemon, only manual on-demand scans are possible.
clamav.no_scan_log: No ClamAV scan log found — last scan date unknown
clamav.no_scan_log_detail: No scan log found in standard paths (/var/log/clamav/). -r = recursive scan, --infected = show only infected files (reduces output noise), --log = save results for audit trail and future diff comparisons.
clamav.scan_very_old: Last scan was {days} day(s) ago ({date}) — very overdue
clamav.scan_very_old_detail: Crypto miners, backdoors, and web shells do not announce themselves. Without regular scanning, infections can establish persistence and persist for months undetected. -r = recursive, --infected = infected files only, --log = save results.
clamav.scan_old: Last scan was {days} day(s) ago ({date}) — consider running a new scan
clamav.scan_old_detail: Monthly scans leave a large detection window. Weekly scanning is recommended for systems that handle files from external sources or are exposed to the internet. -r = recursive, --infected = infected files only, --log = save results.

ntp.not_enabled: NTP time synchronisation is not enabled
ntp.not_enabled_detail: Without NTP, the system clock drifts over time. This breaks TLS certificate validation, corrupts log timestamps (making incident analysis unreliable), and causes authentication failures in protocols that depend on time (Kerberos, TOTP/2FA). Enable systemd-timesyncd (lightweight, built-in) or chrony (more accurate, recommended for servers).
ntp.not_synchronized: NTP is enabled but the clock is not yet synchronised
ntp.not_synchronized_detail: The NTP service is running but has not completed its first synchronisation. This is normal immediately after boot or on a freshly installed system. If it persists, check connectivity to the NTP pool and review: journalctl -u systemd-timesyncd or chronyc tracking.
ntp.not_synchronized_reason: NTP enabled but not yet synchronised

smtp.exposed_detail: Port 25 open on all interfaces means any host on the network (or internet, if not firewalled) can attempt SMTP connections. On a workstation or internal server this is almost always unintentional and allows relay testing, VRFY enumeration, and spam delivery attempts.
smtp.exposed_reason: SMTP port 25 bound to {bind} — reachable from the network

auditd.not_installed_detail: auditd records system calls and file access events to a tamper-evident log. Without it, privilege escalation attempts, credential file access, and sudo abuse go completely unlogged. Install auditd and configure watch rules on sensitive files.
